items.body: Mount Analogue is a landmark work from a master artist in tribute to the great chain of influence that goes from one seeker to another, from one artist to another. I consider it another essential clue in my own quest for discovering an applying obscure knowledge. Climbing the symbolic peaks of René Daumal‘s unfinished Mountain Mount Analogue by Bill Laswell + P.St (featuring N.P. Molvaer, H. Kaiser, P. Howard, G. Haynes, P. Apfelbaum…)   I remember the first time I bought music by Bill Laswell. It was 1998, my last year of high school, and I was in Cleveland with a friend on a spring break road trip fueled by punk rock shows and NoDoz. Record stores were an important part of that trip too, and I remember finding a section of CD’s marked “Bill Laswell” and I was intrigued. I picked up a CD called Jihad (Points of Order) by one of his voluminous side projects, Automaton. It consisted of two long tracks, each around 23 minutes. The album featured musician Tetsu Inoue whose name didn’t mean anything to me then, though now it occupies a special place in my long-term love affair with ambient music. It also featured Lili Haydn on violin, and Nicky Skopelitis, a frequent collaborator with Laswell, on guitar. In my opinion, Skopelitis could get a lot more love for his expressive guitar work then I’ve seen. Of course, Bill Laswell was also on the record providing bass, electronics, treatments, and without question, his expansive musical vision. It was the beginning of a journey into his wide-ranging musical world. I started keeping my eyes and ears open for anything Laswell had his hand in, and as I would soon find out, his hand was in all kinds of interesting material; and Material happened to be the next group of his I discovered. The next real gateway drug, however, was the double album under the Axiom Ambient moniker, Lost in Translation. With song titles like “Cosmic Trigger” how could one go wrong in picking up an album like this unheard? It was around the same time I was reading deeply across the works of Robert Anton Wilson, and his book Cosmic Trigger had set me off on my own quest for Sirius. There is also a song on that record called “Holy Mountain” which brings us to the present album, Mount Analogue, marking yet another vast peak in Laswell’s long career. There is a connection between that song and this album. This musical journey pays tribute to René Daumal and his enchanting world of mysteries and magic. The album shares its title with Daumal’s novel, Mount Analogue: A Novel of Symbolically Authentic Non-Euclidean Adventures in Mountain Climbing, published posthumously in 1952, eight years after the author’s untimely death. Another connection that encompasses Laswell’s singular talent as a sound sculptor and practitioner of the alchemy of music reconstruction and mix translation, as well as his ability as a studio conductor in bringing the work of disparate musicians into progressive harmony. Lost in Translation featured a vast army of adventurous ambient musicians whose work he fused into its singular form. Inou and Skopelitis both made contributions, as did Terre Thaemlitz, The Orb, and various players from the expanded funakdelic pantheon. The cast of supporting musicians on Mount Analogue is a little bit less than Lost in Translation, but still substantial, and reflects another wave of audio connection and total immersion in contemporary music. Contributors to this poetic musical vision include Bill Laswell (bass), Henry Kaiser (guitar), Anna Clementi (vocals), Percy Howard (voice), Hideo Yamaki (percussion), Graham Haynes (cornet), Dorian Cheah (violin), Nils Petter Molvaer (trumpet), Peter Apfelbaum (keyboard), and P.ST (concept, electronics), who all lend their talents to a series of excerpts from Daumal‘s text. Beyond P.ST, who I’ve written about before, I’m not familiar with the work of these musicians. That in itself is an invitation to discover their other work, expanding the field of musical knowledge and mystico-musical kinship. Finding a CD in a record shop has the possibility of sending a person out on a quest. The references to books and novels, the different artists, all become keys for future exploration when trying to find a way through labyrinthine tunnels of reality. “And what about you? What are you looking for?” Daumal asks. Me? I was looking for the kind of clues Laswell leaves for fellow seekers. Directions for navigating my path out of the labyrinth and up into the foothills towards the ascent beyond. Mount Analogue by Bill Laswell + P.St (featuring N.P. Molvaer, H. Kaiser, P. Howard, G. Haynes, P. Apfelbaum…)   HOLY MOUNTAINS :: Another linking thread is how the song “Holy Mountain” from Lost in Translation, and the first fifty minute piece “Mount Analogue” both deal with the alchemy of ascent. There are many kinds of land formations that humanity looks to for spiritual connection. The forests with their groves of ancient trees and ages of wisdom. The desert with its dry heat and ability to conjure visionary vistas. Rivers without end whose meandering flow bridges the material and immaterial, offering purification and pilgrimage to those who attend their rites. And the mountains, the holy mountains, the high places of the world. All across the world mountains are revered. According to Shinto beliefs Mount Fuji in Japan is the dwelling place of the spirits and deities. Two other holy mountains in Japan complete a trinity of such, Mount Haku and Mount Tate. Mount Kailash in the Ngari Prefecture of Tibet, China is considered the spiritual center of the universe in Hinduism, home to Shiva and Parvati. For Buddhists that same mountain is known as Mount Meru and the place where the deity Chakrasamvara dwells. It is also revered by Jains and in the Tibetan Bon religion, and is considered the place where the first Jain Tirthankara (a kind of savior) achieved liberation and freedom from the wheel of birth and rebirth. In the Bible, Moses had to go up Mount Sinai to receive the Ten Commandments. Yet another link is to the 1973 surrealist mindfuck film Holy Mountain by Alejandro Jodorowsky. The Chilean filmmaker was inspired by René Daumal’s novel Mount Analogue, a book that has held several generations of creators and makers under its spell. The second epic tracks here is “Jodorowsky’s Peradam.” We will get to that, but I want to explore some other correspondences that float into my mind when I listen to this fresh masterpiece. Another person who fell under the spell of Daumal was John Zorn. He has his own album called Mount Analogue as well, out on his Tzadik label in 2012. Zorn is another master at bringing disparate musicians together for magical exegesis of sound. Zorn and Laswell are likewise frequent collaborators with each other. The two have worked on numerous projects including in the band Painkiller. In 2021 they recorded a record together called The Cleansing for Tzadik featuring six songs. The first five songs on that album are dedicated to various mystical, magical and artistic luminaries who have inspired the composers. Included on that record is a song “Alejandro Jodorowsky.” All of this makes sense when you consider that Laswell and Zorn have been friends since the 1970s. That they share similar obsessions and influences should come as no surprise to those who’ve been following along. As Laswell wrote in an interview for the Music Hertz blog, “We have different approaches, but knowing each other for so long has shaped our tastes. While we may have different approaches to music, there is no denying the significant impact of John‘s work on my tastes and creative outlook. On the other hand, you can say he didn’t influence me at all. We just have a great relationship. Our collaborations have been characterized by a sense of mutual respect and a shared commitment to artistic integrity. We understand that the strength of our partnership lies in our differences, and we cherish the creative energy that emerges from our diverse perspectives.” The energy presented on Laswell’s Mount Analogue is of a different point of order than Zorn’s. But they can all be enjoyed together, along with Daumal’s novel, and Jodorwosky’s film. All of this forms a rich creative and nourishing creative stew. Yet Daumal’s novel is short, and it was left unfinished when he died at age 36. Why has this little short novel been so important to so many people? How did it come to be, and how did it come to influence the living masters of Jodorowsky, Zorn and Laswell in the creation of their own epic works? The answer gets into the heart of the mysticism and magic that wind their worth through the creative artifacts manifested by all of these artists. To get to there, we have to take brief detour into the mysterious world G. I. Gurdjieff, a master musician in his own right, and his circle of disciples. Exploring the history of ideas around all this material is very much a huge part of my own enjoyment of the music. However if you want to skip reading these origin stories about Gurdjieff, his friend Alexander de Salzmann who formed a massive influence René Daumal and became a character his novel, you can scroll down to the sections Mount Analogue and Jodrowsky’s Peradam, where I finally talk about the music itself. Mount Analogue by Bill Laswell + P.St (featuring N.P. Molvaer, H. Kaiser, P. Howard, G. Haynes, P. Apfelbaum…)   CIRCLES OF MYSTIC ART :: Zorn’s entire catalog is replete with hermetic, Kabbalistic, mystical and magic iconography, as is Laswell’s. They name drop names and hints in the form of album art with strange symbols and sigils alluding to mysterious figures who have influenced history from the fringes of culture. For those who are in the know, they are in the know. For those who aren’t, curiosity gets piqued, and the quest begins. John Zorn’s album draws inspiration “from the life and work of the towering spiritual figure Georges Ivanovitch Gurdjieff.” The brief liner notes and catalog description doen’t even mention Daumal. Yet Daumal’s book was influenced by his friendship with Alexander de Salzmann, a pupil of Gurdjieff. So why did Gurdjieff have pupils? He wasn’t teaching grade school, but was a teacher of spiritual matters. Hailing from Alexandropol, Yerevan Governorate, Russian Empire (now Gyumri, Armenia) he was of Greek ancestry. As he sought meaning to life went out on a quest in his early adulthood. This quest for wisdom led him to Egypt, Iran, India, Central Asia and Tibet. At the heart of Gurdjieff’s oeuvre was the notion that people aren’t really conscious of themselves and exist in an entranced hypnosis like a waking sleep. Sometimes they wake up for a spell only to fall back in the stupor of slumber, like automatons. Yet having once glimpsed the awakened state, he thought it was possible for people to reach that consciousness again. His search for the means of waking up led him back to ancient truths and wisdom traditions that he thought could help people wake up. It’s my own contention that music made by the likes of Bill Laswell and John Zorn can serve as one of the vehicles for helping people snap out of the trance. Daumal took Gurdjieff’s teaching and put it this way in his novel, “All the means we’ve been given to stay alert we use to ornament our sleep. If instead of endlessly inventing new ways to make life more comfortable we’d apply our ingenuity to fabricating instruments to jog man out of his torpor!” Gurdjieff had seen that torpor in the form of a mass psychosis that had led to the mass slaughter of World War I. He feared that those caught up in the perambulations of a sleepwalker were more susceptible to being controlled by others. (The psychologist Wilhelm Reich would also question the way people voluntarily turned themselves over to one form of authoritarianism after another as explored in his book The Mass Psychology of Fascism. It’s still relevant.) Helping people get out of this trance became Gurdjieff’s life work. Gurdjieff had noted that most people in the past who had wanted to awaken retreated to monasteries, ashrams and hermit caves. This is not really possible for everyone in any society. He also noted that it was usually just one part of a person that got developed in various esoteric schools or sects: their heart, mind or body. He looked for another way, and that way came to be called the “Fourth Way” by his student P.D. Ouspensky who furthered these teachings. The Fourth Way would work on the mind, body and emotions together and in harmony to help bring awakening to individuals. One of those individuals who set out on this path was Daumal’s friend Alexander de Salzmann, from the country Georgia. He was a painter, theater designer and stage lighting artist who counted Wassily Kandinsky and Rainer Maria Rilke as his friends, tapped in to the artistic and spiritual currents of his time. He had been living in Russia but in 1919, because of the revolution, he left with his wife to live in Germany. It wasn’t long after that Gurdjieff and his pupils arrived, and they were introduced by another mutual friend, the Ukranian composer Thomas de Hartmann. The Salzmann’s and Gurdjieff hit it off and they became immediately involved in “the work.” They worked with him as close disciples and collaborators to further it along. After various activities in different countries for several years, Gurdjieff and his followers arrived in France in 1922. It was here that they established his Institute for the Harmonious Development of Man at the Prieuré. The Institute was a place for seekers to live together communally in pursuit of psychic transformation under Gurdjieff who provided both guidance and friction. Conditions were often difficult and hard labor was meted out along with spiritual exercises and practice of art and music. The purpose was to create “conditions in which man could be continually reminded of the sense and aim of his existence by an unavoidable friction between his consciousness and the automatic manifestations of his nature.” Thus begin eight years of intense activity. De Salzmann was painting, his wife was dancing, Gurdjieff went on trip to America and got into a near fatal auto accident. Gurdjieff worked closely with Jeanne de Salzmann in developing movements for her dance, and all of them were trying to keep the Institute running. Yet by 1930 Salzmann had disappeared from the Institute. He felt that Gurdjieff’s attentions to his wife’s dancing were a bit much, while his own considerable talents as a painter had been neglected by his teacher. It seemed to be a bit of a triangle between the master and the married couple. There were rumors that de Salzmann’s son, Michel, might have actually been the son of Gurdjieff, so there may have been something else going on leading to Alexandre’s period of discontent. Whatever the actual case may be, de Salzmann left and joined a monastery, noting that “I had entered … under the name of Brother Petrus. I came out with the title of Father Sogol.” After that he made his living as an antique dealer and interior decorator. Father Sogol was the name given to de Salzmann in Daumal’s singular novel. It was in October of that year that started hanging out at the Café Figon on the Boulevard St. Germain. This was the place where he and the bohemian circle around artist Josef Šíma went to drink after their meetings in Sima’s studio. Daumal, Sima and the others noticed this man, always drinking calvados and writing scripts in Arabic and Chinese. One evening Šíma was struck with recognition for de Salzmann, having previously met him at a publishers event some seven years earlier. He went over to the now familiar man, and introduced the artist to his own circle. De Salzmann later approached them again and after they conversed for some time, asked them to hold their arms out straight to the side for as long as they could, testing them. Some minutes later, Daumal was the only one who still had his arms extended. After this test was completed de Salzmann that he was very taken by the character of Daumal. The two became friends and now the older artist had a younger pupil to transmit the Gurdjieffean gnosis. For Daumal it was a revalation and he became enamored and totally devoted to the work. Mount Analogue by Bill Laswell + P.St (featuring N.P. Molvaer, H. Kaiser, P. Howard, G. Haynes, P. Apfelbaum…)   MOUNT ANALOGUE :: Daumal had already been on his own journey by the time he met de Salzmann. Born in Boulzicourt, Ardennes, France in 1908, by the time he reached his teens he was already known for his precocious avantgarde poetry that was landing him in the leading journals of the time. A literary wunderkind, he came under the spell of Alfred Jarry, who had died the year before he was born. Jarry was a symbolist writer, forerunner of surrealism and Dada, author of the play Ubu Roi, and the novel Exploits and Opinions of Dr. Faustroll, Pataphysician. Daumal came to think of himself as a pataphysician. That is, someone who practices the “science of imaginary solutions,” a philosophical concept created by Jarry. Like other teens, Daumal got interested in the effects of drugs and what they might do to his consciousness. Unlike many other teens, what he messed around with was carbon tetrachloride. This chemical has a direct effect on the central nervous system and in the past was used as a cleaning agent, in early refrigeration systems and fire extinguishers. It was dangerous stuff and got phased out. Daumal wasn’t afraid of a bit of danger, and if taking the drug took him closer to the precipice of death, that was okay with him, because he wanted to see and know what was on the other side. These experiments allowed him to, in his own words, “burst the limits of the possible and projected me brutally into another world.” The lingering after effects of the chemical in his body also might have been one of the contributing factors to his early death at age 36 while he was writing Mount Analogue. He was friends with a group of misfits who were so weird they even got kicked out of the surrealists, which was fine with them because they thought the surrealists and dadaists were too passe. These fellows called themselves Les  Phrères Simplistes or The Simple Brothers, and included the poet and morphine addict Roger Gilbert-Lecomte, the novelist Roger Vailland and another writer Robert Meyrat. They were an inseparable bunch and beyond their shared literary aspirations, they shared a commitment to exploring their consciousness. Bohemians to the core, they were sometimes referred to as “the many headed Rimbaud.”  Together they created the literary journal Le Grand Jeu and put three issues into circulation. The Czech modernist painter Josef Šíma became the artistic director for the publication. It was in the pages of Le Grand Jeu where they denounced surrealism, and in turn had their provisional micro-society in turn denounced by Andre Breton. After Daumal’s encounter with de Salzmann at the Café Figon he increasingly gave himself over to the teachings of Gurdjieff transmitted to him by way of his new friend, and he kept busy writing including a column on pataphysics for La Nouvelle Revue Française. Alexander de Salzmann had already died in 1934, and after his passing, Daumal continued to study and work with his widow Jeananne. She had set up communal homes dedicated to “the Work”, and he worked with her in those settings. By 1938 he was working the work directly with Gurdjieff himself. It was the same year his first novel A Night of Serious Drinking was published. It contains allusions to Gurdjieff’s ideas of being asleep in a dreamlike existence through the metaphor of drunkenness, but it was his second novel, the one he died in midst of writing, that shows the unmistakable influence of Gurdjieff. He started Mount Analogue in 1940. Part of his inspiration was to “do for metaphysics what Jules Verne had done for physics.” Indeed, the book can be looked at as being related to science fiction. It is the record of expedition to climb a mountain that most people in the world do not even know exists, a mountain range that cannot be seen, even though it is the highest mountain range in the world, much higher even than the Himalayas. The books narrator talks about “how it was proved that a hitherto unknown continent really existed, with mountains much higher than the Himalayas; how it happened that no one had detected it before; how we reached it; what creatures we met there; how another expedition, pursuing quite different goals, barely missed destruction; how we have begun little by little to put down roots, so to speak, in this new world; and how, nevertheless, the journey has barely begun.” These are some of the words quoted in Bill Laswell’s masterful musical interpretation of the novel on the first fifty minute side titled after the book. It is a musical work that begins in sections with various spoken quotes from the book. Then he and his fellow musicians come in and explore the meaning of that quote through their instruments. Voice, cornet, and electronic soundscapes drift along a cool breeze in the opening section. Attainment is still far ahead, but there is buoyant joy in beginning the journey. Thin violin lines begin to weave in complex counterpoint with delicate fretwork on bass and guitar. As the music progresses bits start to get processed, glitched, a phrase will skip like a skipping CD snapping the listener out of the trance of sleep and returning them to the present musical moment. Swirls of chaos threaten the first wave of bliss with the panic that comes to any seeker, and from this panic, new ways around temporary obstacles are improvised. Escalating electronic sweeps and swoops climb and rise marking new vistas. A female voice, in keening ululations recalls the female voice on “Holy Mountain” on the Axiom Ambient album, creating a correspondence system of parallel musical symbolism. So it goes on through several movements, each inaugurated by a slowly read quote from the book. Each quote can be heard before sinking into a new phase of discursive meditation along with the music, each section bringing the listener closer to the peak, closer to discovering Mount Analogue itself. Mount Analogue by Bill Laswell + P.St (featuring N.P. Molvaer, H. Kaiser, P. Howard, G. Haynes, P. Apfelbaum…)   JODOROWSKY’S PERADAM :: The second half of the album is dedicated to a series of five intricate solo electric guitar fantasias by Henry Kaiser. The first of these, clocking in at 48 minutes,  is titled “Jodorowsky’s Peradam,” taking us further along the journey. Jodorowsky’s story is as epic as any of the other mystical artists, seekers and musicians already written about whose lives have been touched by the teachings of Gurdjieff. He was born in Chile in 1929 to a family of Jewish immigrants who had fled the pogroms of Russia. When he was 23 he emigrated to France.   It wasn’t long afterwards that he started working in Marcel Marceau’s mime troupe. Jodorowsky started hanging around Breton and his circle. Among many of his other antics, he instigated The Panic Movement, a school of transformative performance art dedicated to the ancient god Pan. In the 1950s and 60s of Paris the circles that had been built up around Gurdjieff in previous decades weren’t just a memory gone with the passing of a remarkable man, but an objective reality. Students were still around. In particular, Jeanne de Salzmann. Not only was she still alive, she lived until she was age 101, passing away in the year 1990. The work continued. (Jodorowsky himself is 97 at the time of this writing.) In the filmmakers autobiography, The Spiritual Journey of Alejandro Jodorowsky, he writes about his relationship with G.I. Gurdjieff’s purported daughter Reyna d’Assia. They had met after a screening of El Topo in Mexico City. There was instant sexual chemistry between them and they went back to her hotel. According to the story they talked about her father and his travels in India while they made love. She went on to transmit to him eighty-two different sayings that she attributed to her father. Jodorowsky wrote these down in his book. Whether or not the eighty-two saying were really part of an oral transmission from Gurdjieff to d’Assia to Jodorowsky, I’m not sure matters. They are worthy of meditation and contemplation. I tend to believe the story myself. From his fertile mind came his film Holy Mountain. Jodorowsky has always been forthright and clear on his influences, and he acknowledged how reading Daumal seeded aspects of his film into his mind. Like anything else that Jodorowsky came across, whether it was learning painting from Leonora Carrington, or taking sacred mushrooms with María Sabina, or practicing Zen Buddhist meditation with his master Ejo Takata, he was never content to simply let any one of them be end of his own spiritual quest. He kept on seeking even as he learned from these individual masters and used that knowledge to become his own master, acknowledging the genius in them, but never bowing down to any of them alone. Even so, the fingerprints of Gurdjieff and Daumal are all over his film Holy Mountain. In this movie Jodorowsky plays the roles of an alchemist to a messianic figure who has come in search of knowledge, joined by a group of figures representing the seven planetary archetypes. The alchemists puts these seekers through a series of rituals that mimic the alchemical process of transformation: calcination, where the ego gets burned asunder, preparing the way for new growth, then dissolution, the soul now untethered, into separation where different parts are further purified from one another before being brought back together again in conjunction, followed by further distillation, all culminating in the in the final stage of coagulation, the creation of the philosophers stone, inner gold. As their identities are stripped away and reforged they head to the summit of the Holy Mountain, the summit of true of knowledge, of final enlightenment. Yet in the end even this attainment is seen to be illusory. After reaching the final rung of one ladder, comes the realization that they are once again at the bottom of another. In the final part of the film, the camera turns towards the audience and the alchemist implores everyone to awaken. “Real life awaits.” It is here in this world that at our spiritual efforts must be employed. A peradam is a kind of crystalline stone described in Daumal’s novel. They are described as being  “a clear and extremely hard stone… a true crystal… harder than diamond.” A person could only discover a peradam through intense inner work. Those who sought the higher realms would be gifted with one after peak moments of realization. For the mountain guides who took people to Mount Analogue a peradam was the only payment they would take. The guitar fantasia here is a true peradam, a manifestation of intense effort and dedication to the inner work of musicianship and artistic vision. It continues on the next four shorter tracks completing this magnum opus, “The Door To The Invisible Must Be Visible,” “The Alchemist,” “21 May 1944” (this track a tribute to the day of Daumal’s death), and the “Application of Obscure Knowledge.” For those who pick up the album on Bandcamp, a third album length track is available, a remix of first “Mount Analogue” piece by PS.T. It’s a great reinterpretation of the source material and another chance to voyage upwards into liminal verticality. It finds a fitting home on the Sub Rosa label whose expansive catalog peradams in the form of discs, vinyl, and downloads suitable for the seeker who wishes to find a guide for further exploration of landscapes and vistas remain shrouded in mystery. This album is a landmark work from a master artist in tribute to the great chain of influence that goes from one seeker to another, from one artist to another. I consider it another essential clue in my own quest for discovering an applying obscure knowledge. Mount Analogue is available on Sub Rosa. Apfelbaum…)The post Bill Laswell & P.ST :: Mount Analogue (Sub Rosa) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Bill Laswell与P.ST合作的致敬之作，取材于法国作家René Daumal未完成的小说《Mount Analogue》，以一座象征性的神秘山峰为核心意象。乐评人追溯了Laswell的音乐谱系，从早年Automaton项目的氛围电子，到Axiom Ambient系列的迷失太空感，最终抵达这张更具仪式色彩的作品。专辑召集了多位跨领域乐手——小号手Nils Petter Molvær、吉他手Henry Kaiser、鼓手Pheeroan akLaff等——在Laswell的录音室指挥下，将电子音景、即兴段落与世界各地的器乐质感融为一体。Laswell以贝斯、电子处理和混音重构为核心手段，展现出他作为声音雕塑师的独特能力，在不同音乐家之间搭建对话桥梁。这张作品延续了他对神秘主义与形而上主题的长期兴趣，将文学文本转化为可聆听的声波地理学。

items.body: Photographic Memory is essentially the city chopped fine until it stops sounding like a city and starts sounding like weather. It’s made to be heard as a continuous mix, but Speake wants you to feel free to dip in and out. Speake wants you to feel free to dip in and out Photographic Memory by Speake   Speake makes handmade electronic music from London field recordings, home-built instruments, and charity-shop vinyl. Photographic Memory is essentially the city chopped fine until it stops sounding like a city and starts sounding like weather. It’s made to be heard as a continuous mix, but Speake wants you to feel free to dip in and out. The terms eidetic memory and photographic memory are often used interchangeably, a photographic memory refers to the ability to recall images, text, or objects in extreme detail with high precision after seeing them only once. Vivid mental imagery somehow impacts people’s ability for “mental time travel,” or the ability to remember past events as well as imagine future events. It is said that extensive research has failed to demonstrate consistent correlations between the presence of eidetic imagery and any cognitive, intellectual, neurological, or emotional measure. Perhaps we have developed an ability to organize certain types of information, rather than possessing an innate total recall or eidetic ability. Listen up, see what you think. “I mark but the hours of sunshine” (6:49) opens, and first something is happening in a big empty wet room, a strange munchy beat emerges, not exactly hypnotic but it does repeat in a seductive mind altering way. The liberating percussion takes away any negativity, the core stays while constantly new bits appear to add variety and sunshine, now we are building a groove. Searchlights claw the dark circle of ancient ruins :: I would like to eat sheets of rice noodles right now, stuffed with various essences, known as Cheung Fun, so smooth, slippery, soft and chewy. “No cheung fun after 5pm” (3:19) starts with a renegade commando beat, and soon the whole band moves in, bringing a blend of percussion, keyboards, odd strange sounds that repeat, a skeletal electronic clock, rumblings, and some surprise bottle play moments. “Have you ever been on a boat when you couldn’t see the land?” (5:36) Starts with ticking. Perhaps we are standing near the engine when crossing the Pacific ocean on a new kind of liner, listening to the shoveling of coal and soon a constant very steady machine is running with odd flickers of voices or phantoms. When the flow takes it down to the skeleton, soon the percussion brings it up again. Are we rowing now? Bonny hand knocks create the beat, at times someone is tossing coins or seeds or pebbles, and the machine is always running, until the arrival. This time, the motor starts right away and so we head out, “A pregnant pause” (1:40) flows along and then abruptly everything changes. “When did you stop dancing?” (8:54) enters with simulated sizzling hand tapped percussion and some electronic sparks and flares. I remember the sound made when the stylus gets to the end of the record, the vinyl windoff sound goes on and on with a hint of high hat that keeps the forward motion spicy and strong. This is followed by a title that sounds uncomfortable, “Pushing on the bit that hurts” (4:54). When the track starts, things are dark, until the sizzle walks up and away we go. The wind blows over desolate ruins and searchlights claw the dark circle of ancient ruins. I imagine riding a bike carefully down a very steep and long rocky mountain ridge at night. Sometimes the dripping sounds electronic. The crickets are playing with dry bones, tapping out musical messages, “Passing moustaches through the fence” (4:30), the piano makes this very different from what has come so far. There are Martians imitating dripping water in the cave, soon the percussion gallops along, clanking and reeling. I think there is something in the distance, we are within the machine and in the background is some more music, maybe a circus or a radio saloon. Here the piano never gets to the front and center, the clicks own us, and the crickets with those tapping bones. The final track, “Photographic Memory” (31:45), in fact is also the title track, and it turns out to be the whole album reprised as one long piece. The segues are invisible. Photographic Memory is available on Bandcamp. Photographic Memory by SpeakeThe post Speake :: Photographic Memory (Self Released) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以伦敦田野录音、自制乐器和旧货店黑胶为素材，将城市声响切碎重组，模糊了城市与天气之间的听觉边界。Speake 采用非连续混音的发布方式，邀请听众随时切入或退出。评论以'照相式记忆'为隐喻，将eidetic imagery（遗觉像）概念与音乐结构对应，探讨片段化感知如何重组为心理漫游。开篇曲目以潮湿空旷房间的咀嚼感节奏展开，解放式打击乐逐步叠加成律动；中段曲目引入骷髅式电子钟声、瓶罐敲击与机械运转声，模拟渡轮航行中的感官漂移。每首作品如同压缩的城市切片，节奏在骨架与血肉之间反复切换，自制声响与循环元素交替推进，形成一种冥想式的即兴叙事。手工制作的美学与城市田野采样的结合，使整张专辑在实验电子、声音拼贴与氛围音乐之间建立了独特的联结。

items.body: Review by proto-baldrick — The question seems to be, what differentiates this outstanding release from a Thinking Plague album? Many of the same elements are present'first of all the compositional style. Johnson's extremely distinctive and sophisticated approach to harmony and counterpoint is in evidence, where layers grate and glide against each other, disorienting the listener until background elements come to the surface and reveal the controlled and balanced design. There is also his typical fearlessness in breaking the flow with a sudden change in density and orchestration, which nonetheless maintains the tension and drive. One obvious point of distinction is the increased presence of 'classical' instruments (strings and winds), but (contrary perhaps to his intent) the overall impression is still of an expanded rock band sound rather than a rock composer's attempt at orchestral music. I find this to be a merit rather than a shortcoming.I suspect it has something to do with the people involved (though I'm never quite sure who is 'in' Thinking Plague). This relates to the orchestration and method of production, which necessarily relies heavily on remote recording as opposed to live-in-the-studio. There is also a deliberate attempt to more freely explore Johnson's classical influences. These are hard to pin down, though he has cited William Schuman as a reference. To my ear there are fleeting references here to Henri Dutilleux, and maybe even to some film composers such as Jerry Goldsmith. At times the genre approaches classical art song.The musicians are absolutely topnotch and fully up to the task of interpreting this weighty music. The rhythm section in particular is both solid and beautiful. The brass and strings shine and soar, while sitting organically in the overall texture. I have a slight issue with the vocals, which I have also noted with later Thinking Plague releases. Although much credit is due to Elaine DiFalco for her longstanding commitment to Johnson's music (how many singers would take this on?), I constantly have the impression that she is auto-tuned. It's possible that this is just a quality of her voice, but I can't help doubting it. In any case, this quality detracts ever so slightly from the organic quality of the music. It also has a bit of an obscuring effect on the lyrics, which nonetheless seem to convey a politically progressive, environmentally conscious stance (as with many Thinking Plague songs).Overall, this is a great work by (in my view) a very significant and high-level composer, not just within progressive rock but generally. My rating reflects this rather than any speculations about or imperfections in the components.
items._genre: avant-prog / chamber rock / contemporary classical
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑延续了Mike Johnson一贯的复杂对位与和声风格，层次在摩擦与滑动间制造听觉错位，低频元素浮出表面时揭示出精心控制的平衡结构。弦乐与管乐的加入拓展了传统摇滚乐队的声响边界，虽未完全进入交响化写作，仍呈现出被扩展的室内摇滚美学。制作依赖远程录音，使得配器与编曲层次极为丰富。古典影响隐约可辨，评论者提到Dutilleux、Goldsmith乃至艺术歌曲的影子。节奏组扎实而优美，铜管与弦乐在整体织体中有机穿插。人声方面Elaine DiFalco的演绎略有自动调音痕迹，稍损有机感。歌词延续政治进步与生态关怀立场。整体是一部高水准作曲家式的前卫摇滚作品，在编制与和声思维上具有跨领域重量。

items._cn_summary: 本期《The Wire》杂志聚焦多条线索交汇的地下场景。封面人物Space Afrika将俱乐部文化与1970年代地下广播网络相映射，探索声音传播的历史脉络。黎巴嫩作曲家Jad Atoui通过拾取植物与硬盘内部的微观电流，将自然声响与数字信号并置。葡萄牙作曲家Nuno Canavarro回顾其1988年经典专辑《Plux Quba》的创作背景。Lucy Liyou结合韩国盘索里传统说唱与文本转语音技术，探讨身份议题。智利作曲家Darla Quintana将天文学数据转化为声音结构。此外，本期Invisible Jukebox栏目聚焦Royal Trux创始人Jennifer Herrema，Global Ear探访黑潭草根音乐场景，Epiphanies栏目记录Alan Courtis在战时掩体中演奏的反思。Soundcheck部分涵盖Ellen Allien、Kassel Jaeger、Tyshawn Sorey、Jeff Mills、Kelela等跨越自由即兴、电子、噪音与Avant Rock领域的多张专辑评介，整体呈现实验音乐场景的广度与深度。

items.body:
Colour us enchanted with this otherworldly hour of airborne flute, Saw-U, vocal and drum spirits sourced from the night markets, museum shops and cafés of Laos, by Gary Sullivan ov Bodega Pop, who aptly compares them with Laurent Jeanneau’s forays in the same zone of interest for Akuphone & Sublime Frequencies. Check for the uncanny frissons of ‘Lam Cheung’ and its slew of piquant percussive works, all shimmering with the type of timeless lustre we’ve come to expect from Sullivan & DINTE’s magpie picks...

"In Lao PDR, music was seemingly everywhere. Walking through an open field outside Savannakhet to the sound of someone playing a khaen on a distant porch, the bracing rush of electronic molam from of one of Vientiane’s many aging malls, the awkward blending of the blind so u player’s voice with the bustling sounds of Luang Prabang’s night market.

It was in that UNESCO World Heritage Site that I found most of the CDs and CD-Rs from which I’ve ripped the tracks for this compilation. I’m almost certain I picked up a thumb drive at the night market that held many hours of additional music that could have been included, but if so, I’ve misplaced it, lost it for good, or simply misremember purchasing it in the first place. What I do remember is that these discs were literally the last copies in the cafe, museum, bookstore, and night market where I bought them, and not all of them played all the way through without sonic deterioration.

The sounds compiled here play in stark contrast to the more contemporary recordings I found in Laos, most of which featured some form of upbeat digital workstation molam or children’s songs. In addition to the ever-present khaen, this collection includes recordings of the sanai, a single-reed instrument fashioned from a water buffalo horn, the ceremonial khong nyai gong, the pi and similar free-reeds, and at least a dozen more traditional instruments played by Lao and ethnic minority artists. While some of these tracks were laid down in Vientiane or Luang Prabang, most were recorded near where the artists lived, from the legendary Vat Phou in the far south to the former Pathet Lao capital Xam Neua in the northeast.

Unlike Laurent Jeanneau’s more focused Lao collections for Akuphone and Sublime Frequencies, which remain among my favorite albums of all time, the present cassette-only selection is literally all over the PDR map. The sequencing is entirely in response to rhythm and texture and includes recordings from the 1970s, 80s, 90s, and early aughts. This may frustrate those with more of an ethnomusicology bent, but my hope is that the listener experiences something akin to wandering for the first time through this majestic country, encountering the last copies of forgotten recordings one after another, and hearing in these remains fragments of the past and a living musical landscape."

–Gary Sullivan (Bodega Pop)”
items._genre: world music / traditional Lao / folk / field recording
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑由Bodega Pop的Gary Sullivan策划，收录了来自老挝各地的短版区域性发行CD与CD-R，涵盖七十年代至两千年初的录音。素材取自琅勃拉邦的夜市、咖啡馆、博物馆商店与书店，包括许多仅存的绝版唱片。乐器方面以笙（khaen）为核心，辅以水牛角制成的单簧管萨奈（sanai）、仪式用的锣（khong nyai）、笛与各类自由簧乐器，以及老挝与少数民族艺人的传统演唱。Sullivan强调这些录音与当代老挝的数字工作站molam音乐形成鲜明对比，更具原始质感。合辑按节奏与质感编排，地理跨度从南部的瓦普寺到东北部的旧Pathet Lao首都桑怒，旨在让听者体验初次漫步老挝时偶遇遗失唱片的发现感。Sullivan本人的长篇笔记为此磁带版发行提供了丰富的文化背景。

items.body:
The incomparable Winos dial-up a near-future fraught with glitching techno x surrealist folk artefacts supposed by mainman Morgan Buckley and his pal Ben Donohoe, a 12-track guess-again sprawl ranging from Arthur Russell-esque mood music to screwed Aphex jams.

Under the auspices of “Sworx”, an omniscient dialup modem, they parse coded waveforms in a discrete filing system, combing and recombining its data in a dozen buzzing post-techno chimeras and itchy electro jams. It’s instant classic Wah Wah Wino, freakishly playful and exerting odd sidespins on familiar styles and patterns with a ludic moxie that makes all their music so appealing.

The ‘Sworx’ system speaks its piece in a unique voice of detuned twangs and ululating electronic rhythms, shifting mercurial from what sounds like The Necks doing electro with a prepared piano on ‘OpportuniXt’, to a standout electro zinger with early AFXian vocaloids on ‘The System Works’, and Plone-esque key clatter on ‘dxmmy. pxtsy. rolodex’, thru a centrepiece calling to mind Oval’s most sublime on ‘breathwx (half_life)’. 

‘Western_intel [ frontier 2056 ]’ projects an unusually optimist vision of futurism, less techno dread, more cyber-pastoral, and the trip continues to wend from displaced, outernational folk in ‘Langley Prayer Room 9’, to a masterstroke of pitchbent club sauce in ‘sWORxism_noclocks_notimekept’ that tickles rarest pleasure centres with its piquant wrong-notes and gooey groove.

Collect them all!
items._genre: post-techno / glitch / experimental electronic / electro / surrealist folk
items._cn_summary: 专辑《Sworx》由Morgan Buckley与Ben Donohoe以一个名为'Sworx'的拨号调制解调器为概念框架，将编码波形视为可解析的离散文件系统，在十二首作品中不断拆解与重组数据。整体风格在故障化的后 techno 嗡鸣与超现实民谣碎片之间游走，既有接近Arthur Russell式氛围音乐的片段，也有类似早期Aphex Twin的扭曲人声与Plone式的轻快键击。'breathwx (half_life)'以减法式数字处理呼应Oval的美学，'Western_intel [ frontier 2056 ]'则摒弃techno常见的未来焦虑，转向田园化的乐观想象。'Langley Prayer Room 9'融入错位的外来民谣元素，'sWORxism_noclocks_notimekept'则以走调的俱乐部律动制造独特的听觉快感。整张专辑延续了Wah Wah Winos厂牌一贯的顽皮实验气质，在熟悉的类型框架中注入出人意料的变奏。

items.body:
Thee most coveted collection of Coil demos surfaces on CD, opening a window onto the recording sessions for their pivotal 1991 release, ‘Love’s Secret Domain’. 

Originally collated on a demo tape for WaxTrax! records in 1989 under the working title ‘The Side Effects of Life’, these are the raw early iterations of tracks that would become ‘Love’s Secret Domain’, and arguably one of the ’90s definitive albums. Only a handful of the original cassette are known to exist, and have understandably become important artefacts in their own right, so it’s a massive buzz to finally, physically grasp the album in its entirety, here supplemented by material off the ‘Wrong Eye/Scope’ 7”.

Between the album’s two bookending versions of ‘Fidgit’, which later appeared on the ‘WaxTrax! Sampler #2’ tape in 1989, the album spools familiar yet rawer examples of Coil classics such as ‘Dark River’, ‘Teenage Lightening’ and ‘Love's Secret Domain’, each replete with haphazard fades, cuts and stereo bias, and often with lots of ferric noise. However none of that should put prospective listeners off, with results more faithful to the original than the weirdly pitched version found on YouTube and p2p sites.   

Ultimately it’s a proper find for Coil diehards, but anyone intrigued by the hidden reverse of what was going on in parallel to Rave, grunge and post rock in the phase shift between later ‘80s and early ‘90s, should fill their boots.
items._genre: industrial / experimental electronic / darkwave / post-punk
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑收录了Coil在1991年正式发行《Love's Secret Domain》之前的原始录音素材，最初以《The Side Effects of Life》为名于1989年汇编为磁带小样寄给WaxTrax!厂牌。原始磁带存世极少，因此此次以CD形式完整呈现显得尤为珍贵。唱片收录了《Dark River》《Teenage Lightening》《Love's Secret Domain》等后来成为Coil代表作品的早期版本，保留了母带处理前较为粗糙的质感，包括随机淡入淡出、剪辑痕迹、立体声偏置以及铁带噪音。两首《Fidgit》分别置于首尾，构成了专辑的框架，曲目均比此前流传于网络的不完整版本更为忠实于原始制作意图。这些录音诞生于八十年代末至九十年代初，与同时期的锐舞、垃圾摇滚和后摇滚形成平行对照，展示了电子工业音乐在主流叙事之外所走的另一条暗线。

items.body:
15th Anniversary Remaster of Barnt’s "Geffen" via Magazine.

"Cologne-based record label Magazine celebrates the 15th anniversary of Barnt’s visionary anthem Geffen. One of electronic music's most defining tracks of the 2010s will be reissued in a 2026 remaster edition, marking the first time it receives its own dedicated standalone release.

Originally published on the legendary Cómeme imprint as part of the Various Artists EP The Power Of Now, the track rapidly became a global phenomenon. Looking back, one can hardly imagine Geffen without the 2010s, or, conversely, maybe even electronic music of that era without it. The composition mirrors the expressive possibilities of bedroom producers at the beginning of that decade—an era where artists could launch tracks into the world and have them resonate through their sheer sonic power, without major marketing efforts.

Barnt remembers: "It was one of my earliest tracks. I had just entered art school and didn't own much equipment. My MIDI keyboard only had two octaves. I would always play notes with my right hand while simultaneously shifting through the octaves with my left. This is how the hook line came to life. The production only consisted of seven or eight stems, and barely any equalizers were used during the mixdown. In hindsight, this sparse approach to production probably made it sound different and is why it hits so hard on big sound systems (while sounding unfinished to some on YouTube). At that time, we were doing a small festival on a playground in the center of Cologne. When I played the CDR there, Matias Aguayo demanded it right after. That is how it ended up on Cómeme."

The release comes with two very Magazine-esque reinterpretations from the label's two other co-founders alongside Barnt: a powerful atmospheric club remix by Jens-Uwe Beyer, and Magazine Hallucination, a wild, collaborative, psychedelic mutation by Crato and Beyer.

Jörg Burger, who already mastered the original track, is also responsible for the mastering of this release."
items._genre: electronic / minimal techno / experimental dance / club music
items._cn_summary: Barnt的《Geffen》迎来15周年重新发行，这首在2010年代初具有标志意义的电子舞曲最初收录于Cómeme厂牌的合辑EP中。文章追溯了创作起源——艺术家在设备极其有限的条件下，仅用两八度MIDI键盘、七到八个音轨且几乎不使用均衡器就完成了这首作品，这种极度精简的制作方式反而赋予曲目独特的冲击力与系统适配性。发行版附带两位联合创始人Jens-Uwe Beyer和Crato的重新诠释：一个偏向氛围化俱乐部混音，另一个则走向迷幻突变方向，延续了Magazine厂牌的实验气质。整体内容既是一份文化档案式的回顾，也揭示了简约美学与大型声场表现力之间的内在关联，为理解2010年代电子音乐场景的演变提供了一份具体的文本切片。

items.body:
One of the UK’s most distinctive filmmakers returns to the sea, replete with his original synth score - as on ‘Bait’ and ‘Enys Men’ - but notably damper, deeply blue; surely evoking fellow Cornish native AFX’s ‘SAW II’, BoC interludes, Mordant Music, classic folk horror OSTs.

Centred around the tale of a trawler that returns, sans crew, to a Cornish harbour years after it was thought lost, ‘The Rose Of Nevada’ typically draws on what Mark Jenkin knows best - the people, places and metaphysics of the Atlantic peninsula - whilst ideally emphasising the atmosphere with his special ingredient score. His palette of tape-smudged analog synths feels especially washed out and suggestive of his subject in its briny tone and oceanic scale, which evidently works a treat as a discrete work in its own right, severed from imagery. 

There’s possibly a Kernewek word for “hiraeth”, or “sehnsucht” - a sense of longing, nostalgia - that we’re not aware of, but may perfectly fit the feeling of Jenkin’s music here. Sea-legged loops and sustained drones colour the air with a palpable melancholy in passage from the bittersweet tang of ‘Kneebone Barton’, as used on the trailer, and throughout the album’s patches of decaying wheeze, staining the surface like rust or efflorescence on weathered coves. 

And in the day-dreamiest sense it all fades in/out of consciousness with a perfectly ghostly wow and flutter, as leaching from ‘Through The Gaps’ parts into the slurred whorl of ‘What’s Your Name,’ ephemeral concrète of ‘Look At It’, and final folksy shuffle off into the horizon with ‘Rose of Nevada.’ Here’s looking forward to the film.
items._genre: ambient / analog synth / drone / folk horror OST / concrète
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是英国电影导演Mark Jenkin为其电影《The Rose Of Nevada》创作的原创配乐。Jenkin延续了此前的创作路径——以磁带质感的模拟合成器与海洋意象为核心，构筑出潮汐般深邃的氛围。整张作品色调偏蓝、潮湿而辽阔，饱和度被刻意压低，模拟出氧化与盐蚀的纹理。音景中遍布海雾般的持续低音与循环乐句，从预告片曲目《Kneebone Barton》的苦涩甜美，到《Through The Gaps》、《What's Your Name》的眩晕抖动，再到《Look At It》的短暂具体音乐尝试，最终以民谣节奏的《Rose of Nevada》消散于地平线。乐评将其与AFX、BoC、Mordant Music及经典民谣恐怖配乐相提并论，赞许其作为独立聆听作品亦可成立。整体弥漫着对故土康沃尔海岸的怀旧与形而上学沉思。

items.body:
Swedish jazz icon Christer Bothén returns to Black Truffle backed by Ghosted's Oren Ambarchi, Johan Berthling and Andreas Werliin, playing bass clarinet and donso n’goni over the trio's signature kraut-jazz grooves. Hypnotic, trance-inducing biz FFO Natural Information Society, Don Cherry's 'Organic Music Society', Jon Hassell, The Necks.

If you're up on your Swedish jazz, there's no way you won't have stumbled across multi-instrumentalist Bothén. He's still best known for palling around with Don Cherry when the jazz great moved to Scandinavia, even teaching him how to play the donso n'goni, a sacred "hunter's harp" from the Wassoulou region in West Africa that Bothén had picked up when he was in Mali. And he's continued to perform with various local artists and outfits, conspicuously appearing on Ghosted's 2022 debut album just mere moments before Ambarchi's Black Truffle imprint re-issued his lost Afro-fusion classic album 'Trancedance'. Last year, Bothén finally issued his first solo n'goni album and now he's back on Black Truffle with this fleshed-out collaboration with the Ghosted crew, leading Ambarchi's Leslie-cab guitar drones, Berthling's bass and Werliin's drums.

Berthling and Werliin take the lead at first on the title track, hammering out a rotating groove before Bothén lets rip on bass clarinet. And playing a side role, Ambarchi might have the most important presence, using his signature phased, organ-like tones to provide anchoring drones for Bothén's spirited improvisations. He's even more pivotal on 'Antigorite', playing cascading staccato notes over those Leslie moans and creating an rhythmelodic foil for the other three players' more traditional interplay. But it's when Bothén plays the n'ghoni that the album really hits its stride; on 'Lizardite', those buzzing tones offset Ambarchi's crystalline twangs, filling in for Werliin's imposing basslines. It's the moment where everything else just drops into place, creating a structural crescendo before the album careers into darkness on the brilliantly moody closer 'Chrysotile'.
items._genre: spiritual jazz / free improvisation / kraut-jazz / afro-fusion
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由瑞典多乐器演奏家Christer Bothén领衔，与Oren Ambarchi、Johan Berthling、Andreas Werliin组成的Ghosted乐队合作完成。Bothén在低音单簧管与西非唐索恩贡尼琴之间切换，前者是爵士领域常见的管乐器，后者源于马里 Wassoulou地区的猎人竖琴，带有鲜明的西非仪式色彩。Berthling与Werliin以循环律动打底，Ambarchi则用莱斯利吉他调制出相位漂移般的嗡鸣声响，为Bothén的即兴提供锚点。专辑以同名曲开场，经过'Antigorite'的级联断奏推进，至'Lizardite'嗡鸣琴与清亮拨弦的对话达到高潮，最终在'Chrysotile'中沉入暗色调氛围。整体在自由即兴、西非传统元素与欧陆实验声响之间找到平衡，对Don Cherry的Organic Music Society美学做出当代回应。

items.body:
Weirder, wider, knottier and more hypnotic than its predecessors, L'rain's fourth album closes out her opening act with a vivid firework display of canny cultural references, considered observations and, most crucially, heartbreakingly beautiful songs. It's dumbfounding material, the kind of omnivorous, masterful gear that just doesn't come around often enough - a future classic, to put it bluntly, FFO keiyaA, Mabe Fratti, Dawuna, Dijon or even Broadcast.

There's an aura of comprehensiveness that surrounds 'fata morgana'. Taja Cheek has fully broken in her influences and inspirations at this stage and works without hesitation, painting out her experiences of a broken world with a level of insight that's so rare it's almost unparalleled. We already know that Cheek is a forensic listener; 2024's 'I Killed Your Dog' was a chunky "anti-break-up" album that met sorrow head-on with psych rock, indie, classic R&B and haunted folk references, while its predecessor projected Cheek's ambition, embedding shoegaze and ambient influences into a widescreen collage of avant-garde expressions. It wasn't fusion, exactly, it was Cheek's real-world experience - both as an artist and a high-profile curator - inked on thick, deluxe stock in illuminated letters. And the cycle that she began in 2017 with her tape saturated debut comes to a close with 'fata morgana'.

'I Killed Your Dog' was well aware of its lineage, recorded and produced with a level of detail that immediately put it alongside '70s avant-rock and R&B classics, so 'fata morgana' scratches away another layer, making deeper, odder connections. Even the brief 'rumors of light' is anything but throwaway, casually introducing Cheek's voice through a hailstorm of looped interference that's broken up by disarming bouts of silence. This doesn't only slickly establish the record's experimental credentials, it echoes the eerie 'Transmission' tracks on DJ Shadow's 'Endtroducing'. "This is not a dream," a garbled voice memorably stated, and Cheek's utterances hint at the exact opposite, a choppy mess of backmasked syllables, coughs and hesitations that suggest we're being lowered into a surreal fantasy. Fairytale muted piano phrases appear in the distance and 'with time' materializes on the horizon, kinked by buzzing oscillations that blur time just slightly until Cheek's whisper-sung vocals sidestep into the candlelight. 

Already, it's Cheek's most enigmatic track, occupying the confounding spot between an acid-tweaked Laurel Canyon memory, a half-heard gospel standard and Wendy Carlos's iconic 'The Shining' score: beautiful, meaningful and effortlessly cinematic. And Cheek continues to paint outside the lines, concocting half-song 'blue' from tape-mangled brass loops and gunky drum improvisations that she scrapes into a seductive, hazed atmosphere underneath her reverberating chorals. It's tempting to reference shoegaze or dream pop; the end result is similar, texturally at least, but 'fata morgana' is comprised of hardier raw material: minerals crushed by hand from funk, spiritual jazz, reggae, blues and rock 'n roll. That's never more obvious than on the gorgeous 'july 5th', when smudged folk - mixed with screaming feedback and analog bleeps, of course - mutates into a jerky soundsystem banger in its final act, imagining what OutKast's 'B.O.B.' might sound like if Atlanta was swapped out for Kingston.

Then there's the brassy standout 'elmyra', an anthemic start-stop post-pop banger that's part 'Haha Sound'-era Broadcast and part Wire, distorted to a level that would terrify most green-gilled pretenders. All this, and we haven't even mentioned the album's dense, maximalist lead single 'Soulless Cycle', a track that begins with chattering, bit-crushed samples and double-time kicks and lunges towards its glittering, psychedelic wall of sound that stands as an apt metaphor for the melancholy cacophony of contemporary reality. Before the album's done, Cheek slides in a lysergic slow jam ('birthday') and a near-ambient darkjazz diversion ('church of no one'), reminding us that perseverance and resilience is still possible - preferable, in fact.

Seriously, it's one of those albums that reminds you why you started caring about music in the first place, a milestone that's both cognizant of its place in history and hyper aware of the current moment. So, so good.
items._genre: experimental pop / avant-soul / art rock / ambient / electronic
items._cn_summary: L'Rain的第四张专辑是她创作周期的收官之作，将迷幻摇滚、独立摇滚、经典R&B、民谣、氛围音乐等元素编织成一张复杂的听觉拼贴。Cheek以法医般的听觉精度处理各类文化引用，从DJ Shadow的拼贴手法到Wendy Carlos为《闪灵》谱写的标志性配乐，都在她的声音版图中留下印记。磁带失真铜管循环、半音福音标准曲调、反向人声切片共同营造出超现实氛围。专辑不追求融合，而是在艺术策展人的视角下将个人经历与破碎世界的观察书写于厚重的载体之上，每首作品都在实验性与旋律性之间保持平衡，既诡异又心碎地美丽。

items.body:
Dalhous's first demo collection, originally released on Blackest Ever Black back in 2015. RIYL Ekoplekz, Christ or Forest Swords.

Officially established by Edinburgh-based duo Marc Dall and Alex Ander in 2012, the name Dalhous was really just a formality - the duo had already been working on material together, under the name Young Hunting, for years. This is the era that's properly dredged up here, compiling the demos that Ander and Dall originally compiled for an Intergalactic FM broadcast, eventually dubbing it to tape to fill a gap after the release of 'Will to be Well'. And it's good material, especially if you're interested in tracking the project's evolution. Picking up where that other notorious Scottish electronic duo left off when they wrote 'Twoism', Ander and Dall are fascinated by the kind of moods that disappeared when VHS was traded up for DVD. Not completely in thrall to B-movie soundtracks and documentary themes, Dalhous prefer to muddle their sound with rusted industrial grot, amping up the distortion and making sure the beats fall neatly off the grid. At 21 tracks, it's a lot to plow through, but it's tidy listening if you've already exhausted the duo's proper albums.
items._genre: dark ambient / industrial / experimental electronic / EBM
items._cn_summary: Dalhous首张Demo合辑，收录2009至2013年间为Intergalactic FM广播所制作并转录为磁带的早期素材。爱丁堡二人组Marc Dall与Alex Ander在这批作品中展现出对VHS时代氛围的迷恋，将B级电影配乐与纪录片主题混入锈蚀的工业质感，通过加大失真程度与刻意偏离规整节拍网格的手法塑造独特的声景。21首曲目篇幅可观但编排有序，适合已熟悉该组合正式专辑并希望追溯其风格演变脉络的听众。评论将其定位为接续苏格兰电子组合传统的延续者，强调其低保真粗糙质地下暗藏的实验趣味。

Music, and teasing out strands of makina, electro-house, bardcore and trap with combo’s of ludic, recombinant suss & sharp sound design that became their calling card. items.body:
Reissue of the debut by A.G. Cook & Danny L Harle’s earliest duo, Dux Content, initially dispensed on Gamsonite, a predecessor of P.C. Music, and teasing out strands of makina, electro-house, bardcore and trap with combo’s of ludic, recombinant suss & sharp sound design that became their calling card.

Scrolling back to what now feels like a distant world - the up-for-grabs edges of early 2010s - ‘Lifestyle’ maps out formative aspects of the two producers, still relatively fresh from music studies at Goldsmiths, and making their mark in a burgeoning “internet music” scene. Of course they’re both now chart-topping songwriters/producers with credits for Charli xcx, Dua Lipa, Oklou, et al, but here they’re positively bubbling over with wild, yet disciplined, fusions of upfront hard dance with jazz, contemporary classical and pop that, with the benefit of hindsight, place them in a contemporaneous cultural slipstream with likes of Cracksmurf/T C F or James Ferraro, and soon-to-be spar, SOPHIE.

‘Lifestyle’ is the sound of two minds scything thru cultures and sounds they grew up with - Harle coming from a family background spanning his Geordie dad, John Harle’s BBC scores and early taste for makina’s stacked melodies - and bonding over a shared love of Captain Beefheart, Archie Sheep, and Tim & Eric, all evident in their grasp of shiny, commercial hooks and complex rhythm wrapped up with daft grin and wink. Shake a wand anywhere and you’ll hit a mad one, from the crazed midi piano house of ‘Voice of an Angel’, thru the jazz-fink of ‘City Break’ and ‘Hero Next Door’, free wheeling jazz trance of ‘Heart of Death’ and pitch bent panpipes of ‘Business Class’.
items._genre: experimental electronic / hard dance / pop deconstruction / glitch
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是A.G. Cook与Danny L Harle早期二人组Dux Content的首作再版，最初通过PC Music前身厂牌Gamsonite发行。两位制作人当时刚从Goldsmiths音乐系毕业不久，在2010年代初的互联网音乐场景中探索，将makina、electro-house、trap、bardcore等风格与爵士、当代古典、流行音乐进行大胆而严谨的拼接。曲目如疯狂midi钢琴house的《Voice of an Angel》、爵士trance的《Heart of Death》、弯音排箫的《Business Class》展现了两位创作者在文化与声响上的杂食性——从家庭背景中的Geordie父亲BBC配乐、makina的叠层旋律，到对Captain Beefheart与Tim & Eric的共同热爱。整张作品以荒诞感包裹复杂节奏与明亮流行钩子，成为PC Music美学的早期雏形，也是理解后续Charli XCX、Dua Lipa等流行制作走向的重要考古文本。

items.body:
Picking up where 2024's 'Trash Can Lamb' left off, Keith Freund blurs the line between acoustic instrumentation and DIY electronics on his latest full-length, unraveling his gentle, jazzy sessions with 8-bit beats and oddball FX.

Since the beginning, Freund has been fixated on the character of a sound rather than what that sound, on its own, might represent. His piano parts rarely come off as if they've been played by hand; after chopping them to shreds, he inevitably reconstitutes them into player-piano style impossible sequences, re-organizing the notes and re-sculpting the tone completely. On 'Over Sidewalk Bryum', for example, it's the piano that provides the track's rhythm, accented by radio interference and bit-crushed oscillations. And although Freund does less chipping at his horn parts, letting the sax soar over the chattering electronics, it's still subtly tweaked - nothing's ever quite what it seems.

A swamp of discarded blips and glitches help prop up 'I'll Find a Place for Us', and Freund's soft woodwind tones make their way through the noise initially - or at least that's what we're supposed to think. In time, Freund's sax emerges and the soft-hued, woodwind-like sound is revealed to be a red herring. But that's the kind of sleight of hand that Freund seems to revel in, creating glitchy, unstable music from soft, placid sound sources, not the harsh digital detritus you'd expect to find on a Mille Plateaux disc.
items._genre: experimental jazz / electronic / glitch / DIY
items._cn_summary: Keith Freund延续了2024年《Trash Can Lamb》的创作思路，将原声乐器演奏与DIY电子手段深度融合。钢琴部分被切碎重组，呈现出自动钢琴般不可能的音列；萨克斯声部虽被保留更多原始质感，但仍然经细致处理。8-bit节拍与古怪音效贯穿全作，构成一种温暖却不安定的声响结构。Freund关注的并非声音自身的含义，而是其性格特征——他擅长以柔软、平静的声源制造出不稳定的故障音乐，欺骗听者预期。在《Over Sidewalk Bryum》中钢琴承担节奏功能，伴随无线电干扰与比特压缩震荡；《I'll Find a Place for Us》则以废弃的电子杂音支撑，表面似木管实为萨克斯，制造听觉错觉。整体制作呈现出强烈的手工感与实验态度，独属于作者的声音美学贯穿始终。

items.body:
Recorded live in Brooklyn, 'Somewhere in the Wind' is Loren Connors & David Grubbs’ third album and their first as a guitar duo, showcasing their free-er, noiser side with two extended, ecstatic jams. 

Thankfully, we didn't have to wait another two decades to hear Grubbs and Connors collide again. Their first album, 'Arborvitae', appeared way back in 2003, not long after the duo had first met when Connors shared a bill with Gastr del Sol. But it wasn't until 2024 that they rekindled that magic, shaking things up a little and swapping roles on keys and guitar, with Connors even moonlighting on drums. 'Somewhere in the Wind' might be the perfect companion to that record, recorded last year at Blank Forms, it's their first session featuring both players on electric guitar and it's a joy to engage with on every level. Both distinctive players carry an unmistakable signature style, complementing each other by leaning into the noise and freedom of their collaboration in a way we hadn't witnessed until now. 

If their first two records dug into crepuscular space, the domain of Roy Montgomery and Harold Budd, this one takes its cues from the physicality of their instruments and the knowledge they've acquired along the way. You feel as if you're practically in the room with them as Connors's blurry post-blues recitals casually interact with Grubbs' obsessively tuned intonations. On the first side, we walk into what might as well be a prayer, each note played in reverence to something or someone. But as the piece accumulates weight, so too do the notes, lovingly distorted and pushed off track until all that's left is raw emotion. On the flip, the duo sound even more possessed, kicking up the energy so the notes bounce around the very edges of the recording space. It's a document of two players who don't have anything left to prove.
items._genre: experimental / free improvisation / avant-garde / electric guitar duo
items._cn_summary: 这是Loren Connors与David Grubbs的第三张合作专辑，也是两人首次以双电吉他编制录制的作品，在布鲁克林现场录制完成。乐评指出，前两张专辑偏向黄昏氛围式的空间探索，而这张则转向对乐器物理性的直接表达。Connors模糊的后蓝调语汇与Grubbs精细调音的演奏形成互补，两人相互推动，滑入更为嘈杂、自由的领域。专辑分为两面：第一面如同一段祷文，音符逐步积累重量，被推向失真直至仅剩原始情感；第二面则更具能量，音符在录音空间的边缘反弹。评论认为这是一份两位艺术家无需再证明任何东西的记录，展现了长期积累后的从容与默契。

items.body:
Recorded last year, 'Lynboril Linsinopril' is a lengthy session from seasoned improvisers Adam Bohmen (on strings and amplified objects), Sue Lynch (on woodwind) and Crystabel Efemena Riley (on percussion).

All members of London's Horse Improvised Music Club, Bohmen, Lynch and Riley are motivated by the act of playing, something that's evident immediately. There's a refreshing freedom to their approach; it's relatively straightforward free improv gear, with Riley's tuff rhythm section providing an anchor for her collaborators' wildest skronk-y expressions, but breathes outside of the usual boundaries, never falling into the expected locked grooves. If you follow Cafe Oto's orbiting improv scene, this'll be worth a closer look.
items._genre: free improvisation / avant-garde / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是伦敦Horse Improvised Music Club三位即兴音乐人的长时段录音作品，Adam Bohman负责弦乐与放大物体、Sue Lynch演奏木管乐器、Crystabel Efemena Riley负责打击乐。整张作品以自由即兴为核心驱动力，乐手们从演奏行为本身获取创作动机，呈现出一种清新的自由感。Riley坚韧的节奏段落为其他两位乐手的狂野声响表达提供支点，三人组合在传统自由即兴框架之外寻找空间，避免落入常见的固定模式循环。整张专辑的音乐语言充满探索性，既有明确的结构锚点，也有充分的自由延展空间。对于关注Cafe Oto周边即兴音乐场景的听众而言，这是一张值得细听的录音，展现了伦敦地下即兴社群活跃的创作状态。

Building on a decade of work spanning cuts for Brownswood thru to jams with Matthew Herbert and Matt Davies, ‘Arc’ finds Yorkshire-bred artist Barley fully indulge formative passions for microt
items.body:
On Kirk Barley’s definitive solo gem, alternative tunings and a tactile feel for pitching rhythms generate their gentlest and most absorbing work, twinkling amid a microcosm of similar, exploratory productions from Mark Fell & Rian Treanor thru to Aleksi Perälä, Beatrice Dillon, Terry Riley & Jon Hassell.

Building on a decade of work spanning cuts for Brownswood thru to jams with Matthew Herbert and Matt Davies, ‘Arc’ finds Yorkshire-bred artist Barley fully indulge formative passions for microtonal just intonation - as seeded in Terry Riley’s ‘Shri Camel’ - and slippery syncopation to the fullest. Half solo, proper, and half peppered with percussion by regular spar, Matt Davies, it follows his nose for open frontiers of alternative tunings and wonky meter with the blend of low key modesty and prism-pushing tekkerz that have long endeared his work to lovers of lower case experimental music. 

Sweetly balanced between timeless, folk-soul-wise and futurist sensibilities, the half hour suite knits hyaline synths and rippling gamelan metallophonics with clarinet and guitar in lissom, sloshing shapes that effortlessly seduce, rather than demand, the listener’s attention. In particular we are drawn to the bits in duo with Davies, floating sublime ideas in the dreamlike, inverted dub architexture of ‘Ion’, settling on mind like a strangely bucolic Incus work on ’Sundry’, and thru the exquisite, tip-toed rhythms of ‘Ecstatic’, to a trippier, bittersweet type of ante-chamber music on ‘Fret (Hear)’.

He’s also deeply charming when left to his own devices. Ambient opener ‘Billow’ calls to mind the tenderness of Cotton Goods works, and ‘Knead’ chases a certain geist of Irdial or Plaid-esque gamelantronica into the sublime title tune, while ‘Prism’ most beautifully ties all his interests in a melting dream sequence which he caps with the harmonic nightlight glow of ‘Column’.
items._genre: experimental / microtonal / lowercase / ambient
items._cn_summary: Kirk Barley的专辑《Arc》展现了微型调式与非常规节奏律的深度融合。作品以特里·赖利《Shri Camel》为灵感源头，运用纯律微分音体系与滑动切分节奏，将合成器、加美兰金属打击乐、单簧管与吉他编织成流动的半小时组曲。专辑一半独奏，一半与鼓手Matt Davies搭档，'Ion'以倒置dub空间漂浮，'Sundry'展现如Incus厂牌般的梦境质地，'Ecstatic'以轻盈步态勾勒节奏。独奏部分如'Billow'柔和如Cotton Goods之作，'Knead'追踪Irdial或Plaid式的加美兰电子脉络，最终'Column'以泛音夜灯般的微光收束。整张专辑以低调谦逊的触感探索调律与节拍的开阔前沿，定位介于民俗永恒感与未来主义之间。

items.body:
Anyone obsessed with those two incredible ‘Begena Songs…’ comps on Death Is Not The End will be properly enchanted by this more expansive - yet still intimate - suite of snapshots from Ethiopia, 1971, spanning the unique, twanging harp sound thru to Amharic poetry, chants, and spellbinding flute dances...

One that catches the breath with seldom felt sensations, ‘Ethiopian Musics 1971’ patently owes as much to the incredible performers as their faithful representation in Ragnar Johnson & Ralph Harrisson’s recordings. All secreted to tape on a Uher Report L stereo reel-to-reel recorder, they epitomise an era of ethnomusicological preservation, when the likes of labels such as Lyrichord and  Folkways were already decades deep “in the field”, documenting long-held traditions practically untouched by an encroaching, western modernity. And perhaps most crucially, the recordings beautifully render the acoustic settings and vivid vibes with an immersive quality in stark opposition to the era of dry, so-called audiophile studio recordings of ethnic musics to come - all the better for immersing in this wonderfully unfamiliar world.

The abundance of singular tones and strong, rare feels they produce is quite staggering to our northern english ears, and we reckon also for anyone else, for that matter. Opening to a joyful couplet of a bluesy ’Song about the beauty of women’, and the almost shanty-like swing and hard rhythm of ’Tej Beit Song’, the set reels to distinctive pieces of Ethiopian Christian song set to begena, or ‘Harp of David’, buzz, and a landscape-scale, 13 minute ‘Love Song (Mary Armede)’. A gripping ‘Drum Song (Jigsaw)’ will be mana to rhythm fiends, and a number of standout flute pieces reprise the frisson of our first encounter with this discipline on Sublime Freq’s ‘Staring into the Sun - Ethiopian Tribal Music’ set of 2012, most potently on the pluming twin pipes of the ‘Fila Flute Dance’ parts, whilst the pentatonic craar (6-stringed lyre) parts surely strike nerves for lovers of the rawest blues, and hail the liberated legacy of Mary Armede, a folk singer-fashion designer of Azmari heritage who surely warrants further investigation. 

No doubt this is one of the most striking archival discoveries of 2026, acutely advised to anyone enchanted with music from this corner of the world from Éthiopiques to begena harp, thru to Ragnar Johnson’s other arenas of research for Ideologic Organ in Yemen or Papua New Guinea. Dive in without delay.
items._genre: ethiopian folk / field recording / archival / traditional
items._cn_summary: 1971年由Ragnar Johnson与Ralph Harrisson使用Uher Report立体声开盘录音机在埃塞俄比亚实地采集的系列录音，涵盖贝格纳竖琴、阿姆哈拉语诗歌、咒语吟唱、长笛舞曲等多种传统形式。录音以高保真度保留了真实的声学环境与现场氛围，与后来干燥的录音棚式民族音乐制作形成鲜明对比。开篇以女性赞美歌曲与节奏感鲜明的Tej Beit歌曲引入，随后展开基督教竖琴音乐、13分钟的爱情叙事长歌、鼓乐独奏、双管长笛舞曲及六弦里拉琴演奏。Mary Armede作为阿兹马里传统的女歌手同时身兼时装设计师身份，其遗产在此次档案再发现中获得关注。评论将本辑视为2026年最具分量的档案出版之一，与此前Death Is Not The End厂牌发行的Begena Songs系列构成互文。

items.body:
Thee darkest, weirdest dub perennial from Keith Hudson, 1979, blooms on vinyl for first time in years, ready to scatter smoke and minds into the late and early hours...

First released in 1979 and highly in-demand ever since, the dub sibling to Keith Hudson’s ‘Nuh Skin Up’ pushes that album’s already stark blooz and The Soul Syndicate’s deadly riddims hard into the echo chamber with a balance of experimental nous and heads-down grooves that has assured its place in the pantheon of the most haunting dubs. 

Out of print for decades until a 2007 pressing spiked it back in the water table, the album firmly holds up nearly a half century since its original release on the basis of a future proofed minimalism that continues to haunt successive generations with its bony percussion and a dematerialised soul exemplary of dub metaphysics at its transcendant best.

Up there with the likes of Lee ‘Scratch’ Perry in terms of his dual role as songwriter and desk-tweaking dub maverick, Hudson really gets inside his own tunes, and The Soul Syndicate’s instrumentals, with the uncanniest insight, turning the likes of its title corker into clouds of pillowy steppers bass and streaking echoic contrails.

The way he inverts the vocals on ‘Ire Ire’ to sound properly wrong-end-of-telescope against the foregrounded crack of congas and spectral organ is just magic, and lays the groundwork for so much dub experimentation to come from the likes of everyone from Rhythm & Sound to Tricky, along with the likes of his spellbinding, skeletal steppers dub masterwork ‘Troubles’.
items._genre: dub / experimental dub / roots reggae / dub poetry / minimalism
items._cn_summary: 这张1979年的dub专辑是Keith Hudson与The Soul Syndicate合作的经典之作，以极简手法将原作的蓝调骨架与乐团的致命节奏推入回声深渊。制作上以缩减的打击乐质地、剥离式的人声处理与弥漫的回响层构筑空灵声场，如'Ire Ire'中倒转的声像与康加鼓、幽灵风琴的对话成为后续实验音乐的范本。编曲在实验直觉与沉稳律动之间维持精准平衡，标题曲以蓬松的低频与绵延回声轨迹营造步进感,'Troubles'则以骨骼般精瘦的骨架呈现dub制作的高度凝练。作为dub谱系中的典范，制作思维跨越世代影响了Rhythm & Sound至Tricky等后辈。

An evergreen.. items.body:
Coltrane’s invigorating ’66 spiritual free jazz salvo - the follow-up to ‘A Love Supreme’ (1965) - is unleashed from the Verve Vault, spotlighting his classic line-up tearing out on templates set by Ornette Coleman years prior, along with more reserved moments of beauty. An evergreen..

"Following the genre-redefining revelations of A Love Supreme in 1965, John Coltrane began a dramatic shift toward spiritual free jazz, abandoning familiar forms in favour of a more abstract sonic palette and bold questions he'd spend the rest of his life and career pursuing. Meditations, released by Impulse! in 1966, continues that emotional throughline while retaining, for the last time in full, the classic quartet that propelled Trane to greatness: pianist McCoy Tyner, bassist Jimmy Garrison and drummer Elvin Jones. (They're further augmented by Pharoah Sanders on tenor sax and additional drummer Rashied Ali.) Meditations pushes Coltrane’s spiritual jazz into heightened realms of energy and abstraction — a powerful document of transformation, intensity, and devotion in Coltrane’s recorded legacy."
items._genre: free jazz / spiritual jazz / avant-garde / improvisation
items._cn_summary: 这张1966年的专辑是Coltrane继《A Love Supreme》之后迈向精神自由爵士的关键转折之作。乐队保留了经典的四重奏配置——钢琴手McCoy Tyner、贝斯手Jimmy Garrison与鼓手Elvin Jones，并引入tenor sax手Pharoah Sanders与第二鼓手Rashied Ali，形成双鼓配置驱动节奏张力。专辑抛弃了传统的调性结构，转向更抽象、更具能量爆发力的声音探索，延续并深化了Coltrane对灵性主题与即兴语言的追求。在Pharoah Sanders尖锐的高频萨克管与双鼓组的复杂交织下，音乐呈现出层层叠加的密度与冥想式的情绪流动。整张唱片被视为Coltrane晚期自由爵士路线的起点，记录了他从结构化即兴转向完全解放的一次重要蜕变。

items.body:
Roping in Pierre Bastien and Mark Cunningham to provide brass, Mike Cooper turns in his most kaleidoscopic fourth world dream sequence to date, drawing on dub and exotica to harmonise with Andrew Pekler's marooned soundscapes...

Cooper admits in the liner notes that although he's often compared with Jon Hassell, it's German painter Mati Klarwein fantastical album covers that always reminded him exactly why he was doing what he was doing. Because Cooper makes music for imaginary places, not tangible soundtracks but half dreamed, half lived experiences that course through his catalog of experiments. And his process has never been quite so vivid as it is on 'Stochastic Parrot', a suite of vertiginous reverberations that are struck through with Cooper's "real and virtual" lap steel twangs, collaged together from samples and field recordings that wobble like heat haze. 

Different pockets of rhythm bash into each other on 'ARCHAEOPTERYX', accompanied by Bastien and Cunningham's spiraling brass improvisations. And Cooper holds the sounds together with his lulling repeated phrases; the hand drums might sound as if they're in conflict with the cycling drum machine crashes, but that's the point - it's not like channeling a dream so much as it's like being subjected to three or four dreams simultaneously. It's the ghosts of jazz fusion being raked over coals at midnight: just tune into 'SUMATRA SAMPHIRE', with its distant animalistic wails and popcorn drums, or the granulized 'HAT YAI', that sounds like the prelude to a druggy ritual.
items._genre: experimental / world fusion / dub / exotica / ambient
items._cn_summary: Mike Cooper 召集 Pierre Bastien 与 Mark Cunningham 贡献铜管元素，在这张专辑中呈现出极为绚丽的第四世界梦境质感。他借鉴 Jon Hassell 的精神，却更强调德国画家 Mati Klarwein 封面所传达的幻象美学。Cooper 的音乐并非为真实地点创作配乐，而是介于梦与经历之间的想象空间。专辑中他使用真实与虚拟的钢棒吉他滑音，叠加采样与田野录音，音景如热浪般摇晃扭曲。不同节奏区块相互碰撞，铜管即兴盘旋其上，手鼓与循环鼓机形成冲突感，犹如同时被三四个梦境所笼罩。曲目中既可听到爵士融合的午夜残影，也有颗粒化的仪式感前奏，整体在 dub、exotica 与环境音之间构建出层次丰富的声响实验。

items.body: Nagoya’s leftfield electronic scene has recently garnered interest from the international music press. This is chiefly thanks to the efforts of producer and all-around scenester Yuya Abe (abentis). abentis has been an associate of Facta & K-LONE’s Wisdom Teeth label since 2021. After a chance encounter with Facta on the platform formerly known as Twitter, Wisdom Teeth featured abentis’ track “Bicycle” in their 2022 compilation To Illustrate. Earlier this year, abentis curated a compilation of Nagoya talent for Wisdom Teeth titled nagoyaka na kaze / 和やかな風 (quiet wind). Entries oscillate from woodblock percussion-fronted minimal house to rootsical UK bass. Now the artist returns with his debut album Dim Grow, the first physical release on his fledgling 2++ label, which he plans to use to promote the Nagoya scene. Dim Grow is fairly short, clocking in at just 41 minutes, but contains enough unique ideas to fill a longer work. “Separate” opens the album with an unhurried cavalcade of brassy splashes and arpeggiation evoking Italian experimentalist Caterina Barbieri. It segues into “In Memories,” the longest piece on Dim Grow at just over nine minutes. It’s maybe too long; physically modeled kalimba dominates the first 90 seconds until the rising tedium is suddenly leavened with bass. A Steve Reich influence looms large for the remaining seven-plus minutes, a twinkling tropical variation on the American minimalist composer’s studied drift between melodic and rhythmic phrases. Especially compelling are the reverberant marimba stabs near the end with a series of showy decay accents—essentially the audio equivalent of crisp serifs. “Far Enough” and “Lune,” channel some of abentis’ Japanese influences, particularly goopy analog synth leads reminiscent of Thousand Knives-era Ryuichi Sakamoto and Haruomi Hosono’s late 70s prog-psych experiments—albums like Cochin Moon and Paraiso that détourned western exotica-kitsch. “Far Enough” is particularly mischievous; one motif is teasing a trap-style snare line only to collapse it into a wash of static. Forays into dance music shade the second half of Dim Grow. The swung 4/4 of “Lune” could earn it a place in a more open-minded house or techno set. “Eachpath” susurrates with the restlessness of 2010s deconstructed club artists like Jam City and Lee Gamble, but grounded in the rhythmic and harmonic grooves of 90s intelligent techno acts like B12, Ken Ishii, and LA Synthesis. “Circulation” is the shortest track on the album and may also be the most dance-oriented: bedroom techno with dubby mallet percussion running in opposite directions over male voices that lie on the threshold of discernibility. It’s easy to envision this music issuing from the soundsystem of a chic Nagoya(ka) sake bar, and if abentis gets his way, audiophile venues the world over. (Marcello Ursic)
